notes.short: Ezekiel shut in his house, a sign of closed ears
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to shut himself inside his house, and says he will be tied with ropes and kept silent until God opens his mouth. One reading takes his being shut in, and the ropes, as signs of how his own people would close their ears and keep him from speaking God's message.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: shut yourself inside your house
figure.means: how his own people would shut their ears and, as far as they could, keep him from giving the Lord's message

notes.evidence: G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) says the shutting up, and the bands, which he takes figuratively, were signs of how Ezekiel's countrymen would close their ears and hinder him from giving the Lord's message, and that a series of symbolic actions foretelling Jerusalem's judgment begins with this verse.
notes.limit: This reading is one writer's. He takes the ropes as a figure of his countrymen hindering him from giving the Lord's message, not as cords truly tied on Ezekiel.

cites.quote: This "shutting up," however, and the "bands" ( Eze 3:25 , used figuratively) were signs of the manner in which Ezekiel's countrymen would close their ears, hindering him as far as in them lay from delivering the message of the Lord. With this verse commences a series of symbolic actions enjoined to the prophet in order to foretell the coming judgments of Jerusalem Ezek. 4; 5.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jerusalem drawn on a brick and put under siege
notes.about: God has Ezekiel draw Jerusalem on a brick, build siege works around it and set an iron plate between himself and the city. Verse 3 names the act: “This will be a sign to the house of Israel.” It foretold the siege the Chaldean army would soon lay to Jerusalem.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: take a brick, place it before you, and draw on it the city of Jerusalem
figure.means: Jerusalem under siege: the Chaldean army would soon surround the city, as the prophet's model showed

notes.evidence: Calvin: God signifies by an outward symbol what the prophet is to utter, the siege the Chaldeans would soon lay. Matthew Henry: signs of the siege of Jerusalem that amounted to a prediction, a sign to exiles who saw it. Adam Clarke: an emblematical representation of what would take place. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes): a vivid picture of the event it foretold, perhaps only told to the people.
notes.limit: The note keeps to verses 1 to 3; lying on his side and the rationed bread follow as further signs. Writers differ on whether the signs were acted before the people or seen in a vision and described to them.

cites.quote: Here God begins to speak more openly by means of his servant, and not to speak only, but to signify by an outward symbol what he wishes to be uttered by his mouth. ... God orders the Prophet to erect towers, then to pitch a camp, and to prepare whatever belongs to the siege of a city, because very soon afterwards the Chaldeans would arrive
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The prophet is here ordered to represent to himself and others by signs which would be proper and powerful to strike the fancy and to affect the mind, the siege of Jerusalem; and this amounted to a prediction. ... This is intended to be a sign to the house of Israel ... both to those in Babylon, who were eye-witnesses of what the prophet did
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The Chaldeans threw such a wall round Jerusalem, to prevent the besieged from receiving any succours, and from escaping from the city. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel - This shall be an emblematical representation of what shall actually take place.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A sign to the house of Israel - This "sign" was not necessarily acted before the people, but may simply have been described to them as a vivid representation of the event which it foretold.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Shaved hair, split in three: Jerusalem's fate
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword, weigh the hair and split it in three: a third burned, a third struck with the sword, a third scattered to the wind, a few strands kept. The hair stands for Jerusalem's people, and verse 12 says how each third will fall.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: shave your head and beard
figure.means: Jerusalem's people cut off by God's judgment: a third by plague and famine, a third by the sword, a third scattered among the nations

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the prophet is himself the sign of Jerusalem's utter ruin. Adam Clarke calls it a new emblem: the prophet stands for the nation, his hair for the people, the razor for the Chaldeans. Joseph Benson calls it an emblematical representation of what would befall Jerusalem. F. Gardiner (Ellicott): the sword is taken for its symbolism, a priest's shaving betokening judgment.
notes.limit: Writers differ on whether Ezekiel did all of this before the exiles, or some of it, such as burning a third of the hair inside the city, only in word.

cites.quote: We have here the sign by which the utter destruction of Jerusalem is set forth; and here, as before, the prophet is himself the sign, that the people might see how much he affected himself with, and interested himself in, the case of Jerusalem ... Ezekiel must not cut off that hair only which was superfluous, but cut it all off, denoting the full end that God would make of Jerusalem.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Here is a new emblem produced, in order to mark out the coming evils. 1. The prophet represents the Jewish nation. 2. His hair, the people. 3. The razor, the Chaldeans. 4. The cutting the beard and hair, the calamities, sorrows, and disgrace coming upon the people. ... 3. And the remaining third part he was to scatter in the wind, to point out those who should be driven into captivity.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: What the prophet is here commanded to do was by way of another emblematical representation of what was to happen to the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem. The hair signified the Jewish people; shaving the hair with a razor, the divine vengeance; the weighing of the hair in the balances, the divine equity
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: The thought is plainly that the prophet is to take a sword, on account of its symbolism, and use it instead of a razor. ... The symbolism was the more marked because Ezekiel was a priest, and the priests were expressly forbidden in the law to shave either the head or the beard ( Lev 21:5 ). The shaving, therefore, of a priest’s head and beard with a sword betokened a most desolating judgment.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Clap, stomp and cry “Alas!”: God's anger shown
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to clap his hands, stomp his feet and cry “Alas!” over the wicked abominations of the house of Israel. The gestures put before the people God's anger at their sin and the ruin coming on them by sword, famine and plague.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Clap your hands, stomp your feet
figure.means: God's fixed anger at Israel's abominations, and the ruin coming by sword, famine and plague

notes.evidence: John Calvin says God adds a sign, since words moved them little; the gesture confirms His word. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls them gestures in token of how God will strike them. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): they make known the LORD's displeasure. F. Gardiner (Ellicott): they show God's fixed purpose. Adam Clarke counts them among the prophet's typical acts.
notes.limit: Writers differ on how much the gestures voice anger at the people's sin and how much dread of their coming ruin; several hold both.

cites.quote: Since, then, words moved them but little, God adds a sign, according to his custom in obstinate cases. He orders the Prophet, by clapping of hands, and by extending his legs and feet, to show that the land was cursed. ... God wishes by this gesture that his word should be confirmed, not for the Prophets sake, but for the sake of the obstinacy of those who were deaf to all words
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Gesticulations vividly setting before the hearers the greatness of the calamity about to be inflicted. In indignation at the abominations of Israel extend thine hand towards Judea, as if about to "strike," and "stamp," shaking off the dust with thy foot, in token of how God shall "stretch out His hand upon them," and tread them down
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Through clapping of the hands and stamping of the feet - the gestures which indicate violent excitement - the prophet is to make known to the displeasure of Jehovah at the horrible idolatry of the people, and thereby make manifest that the penal judgment is well deserved.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To clap the hands and stamp the feet ... is a gesture of strong emotion or earnestness of purpose. The prophet is here directed to use it as indicating God’s unchangeable determination united to a sense of grievous wrong.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Show the utmost marks of thy astonishment and indignation, and dread of the evils that are coming upon them. ... To be consistent, they should copy the prophet in his other typical actions as well as these ... Now all these things, because they were typical and commanded, were proper in the prophet
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Forge the chain”: a sign of the coming captivity
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to forge a chain, for the land is full of bloodshed and the city of violence. The chain is a sign of the captivity to come, when the guilty people would be led away in bonds. One writer also reads it as the chain of a prisoner brought to God's judgment.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Forge the chain
figure.means: the captivity coming on the land's guilty people, led away bound to Babylon

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke calls the chain a type of the captivity. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a symbol of the captivity. Joseph Benson: it foreshows the captivity. F. Gardiner (Ellicott) calls it a symbolic act, here done in word. Matthew Henry says it signified the siege, the captives' slavery, or their being bound over to God's judgment.
notes.limit: One writer holds the chain was only spoken of here, not truly forged. Another reads it first as a prisoner's chain at God's judgment, and also as the siege or the captives' slavery.

cites.quote: the prophet is directed to make a chain, as a type of that captivity, in which both king and people should be led in bonds to Babylon, Eze 7:23-27 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: chain--symbol of the captivity (compare Jer 27:2 ). As they enchained the land with violence, so shall they be chained themselves. It was customary to lead away captives in a row with a chain passed from the neck of one to the other.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Make a chain To foreshow the approaching captivity, when both king and people should be carried in chains to Babylon.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: In the midst of this plain prophecy the strong tendency of the prophet’s mind still runs to the symbolic act; but this can be thought of here only as done in word. The chain is to bind captive the guilty people.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Make a chain, in which to drag the criminal to the bar, and set him before the tribunal of divine justice; let him stand in fetters (as a notorious malefactor), stand pinioned to receive his doom. ... The chain signified the siege of Jerusalem, or the slavery of those that were carried into captivity, or that they were all bound over to the righteous judgment of God, reserved in chains.

notes.short: “Oh, Lord GOD”: Ezekiel cries out for his people
notes.about: As the slaughter he is shown in Jerusalem goes on, Ezekiel, left alone, falls facedown and cries out, “Oh, Lord GOD,” pleading that the remnant of Israel not be wholly destroyed. The cry bursts from dismay and pity for his people.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: Oh, Lord GOD
figure.means: the prophet's dismay and pity for his people as judgment falls on them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ecphonesis, or Exclamation. Calvin says the prophet, as if astonished, exclaims with vehemence and breaks forth into a cry, his fall on his face showing human affection; Henry, that he cried out not in fear for himself but in compassion; Gardiner (Ellicott), that he falls on his face in consternation and pleads for the remnant.

cites.quote: So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected. ... “I fell upon my face, and cried, and said, Ah Lord God (Adonai Jehovah)!” etc.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Now as the Prophet fell upon his face, it was a testimony of the human affection … This is the reason why the Prophet lies on his face, as if astonished, and exclaims with vehemence, Alas! O Lord God … Since, therefore, the Prophet saw that city destroyed, he broke forth into a cry
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: he fell on his face, and cried, not in fear for himself (he was one of those that were marked), but in compassion to his fellow-creatures.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Now it is a city of the dead, and he is left standing alone in the midst of the dead. He falls upon his face in consternation, and pleads that “the residue of Israel” may not be utterly destroyed.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “The city is the cooking pot”: a boast turned back
notes.about: Jerusalem's leaders call the city the cooking pot and themselves the meat: its walls will keep them safe, as a pot keeps the meat from the fire. God turns the picture back on them: the slain are the meat, and “The city will not be a pot for you, nor will you be the meat within it.”

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat
figure.means: the leaders' boast that Jerusalem's walls will keep them safe from the enemy, as a pot keeps the meat in it from the fire

notes.evidence: F. Gardiner (Ellicott) says the princes compared the city to a caldron whose strong walls would shield the people from attack, a figure God turns against them. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) calls it the image of the caldron: they are safe within the walls, as flesh in a caldron is unburned. Matthew Henry takes it as a proverbial expression of the same safety, as God's answer shows.
notes.limit: Some writers add that the leaders were also mocking an earlier prophet's word; the note claims only their boast of safety and God's answer to it.

cites.quote: The princes further confirmed the people in their fancied security by comparing the city to a caldron, the strong walls of which should protect the flesh within it, i.e., the people, from the fire of all hostile attack. In the prophecy of Eze 24:6 this figure is taken up, and a very different application given to it; it is also turned against them immediately in Eze 11:7 .
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: These false counselors promised to their countrymen a sure and permanent abode in the city which God had doomed to destruction. ... The same idea is expressed by the image of the "caldron:" whatever devastation may rage around the city, we are safe within its walls, as flesh within a caldron is unburned by the surrounding fire
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This seems to be a proverbial expression, signifying no more than this, "We are as safe in this city as flesh in a boiling pot; the walls of the city shall be to us as walls of brass, and shall receive no more damage from the besiegers about it than the cauldron does from the fire under it. ... This appears to be the meaning of it, by the answer God gives to it
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Ezekiel packs for exile: a sign of the captivity
notes.about: At God's word, and as the people watch, Ezekiel brings out an exile's bags by day, digs through the wall at evening and carries his things out at dusk on his shoulder. God has made him a sign: “Just as it happened here, so will it be done to them”; they will go into exile.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: pack your bags for exile
figure.means: the king and people of Jerusalem going into exile, the king slipping out at dusk through the wall

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a sign done to the letter, to set the coming judgment before the people. Matthew Henry says the prophet is directed by signs and actions to show Zedekiah's captivity. Adam Clarke: he foretells it by action instead of words. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) calls it a real act and a sign. F. Gardiner (Ellicott): a symbolical action of going into captivity.

cites.quote: Symbol of the Emigration ... the prophet was to depict before its eyes, by means of the sign that followed, the judgment which was approaching; in the hope, as is added in Eze 12:3 , that they might possibly observe and lay the sign to heart. ... cites.quote: In these verses the prophet is directed, I. By what signs and actions to express the approaching captivity of Zedekiah king of Judah ... he must first give them a sign of it, must speak it to their eyes first and then to their ears

cites.quote: In the beginning of this chapter he foretells the approaching captivity of Judah by action instead of words, Eze 12:1-7 . He predicts particularly the flight, capture, captivity, and sufferings of Zedekiah and his followers, Eze 12:8-16
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Bread eaten trembling: the siege's fear acted out
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to eat his bread with trembling and drink his water with quivering and anxiety. Then he is to say that Jerusalem's people will eat and drink in dread, for their land will be stripped bare. His fearful meal acts out the terror of the coming siege.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: eat your bread with trembling
figure.means: the terror and distress in which Jerusalem's people would eat and drink during the siege

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the prophet is again made a sign, expressing Jerusalem's plight in the siege. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a sign of the conquest's terrors, shown by gesture. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a symbolical representation. G. Currey (Barnes' Notes) and F. Gardiner (Ellicott) call it a sign of a siege's terror. Adam Clarke: thus signifying the siege.
notes.limit: Writers differ on whether the meal also pictures scarce food, or only the fear with which food is eaten.

notes.short: A scoffing saying: “every vision fails”
notes.about: People in Israel had a saying: “The days go by, and every vision fails.” The judgment the prophets foretold was slow to come, so they said it would never come. God answers that He will put an end to the saying, for “The days are at hand when every vision will be fulfilled.”

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: The days go by, and every vision fails
figure.means: the judgment the prophets warned of is so long in coming that it will never come at all

original.note: In Hebrew the word for proverb is mashal, a saying current among the people and repeated as if true.

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: the saying had become proverbial; since the destruction had not come yet, they said it never would. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): an unbelieving scoff made a proverb by repetition. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): a saying current among the people; Joseph Benson: a scoffers' saying become proverbial; F. Gardiner (Ellicott): a proverb current in the land.
notes.limit: Verse 27 records a second saying, that the vision is for the distant future; the note keeps to the proverb of verses 22 and 23.

cites.quote: One saying they had, which had become proverbial in the land of Israel ... They said, "The days are prolonged; the judgments have not come when they were expected to come, but seem to be still put off de die in diem—from day to day, and therefore we may conclude that every vision fails ... that because the destruction has not come yet it will never come

notes.short: A coming taunt: “Where is the whitewash?”
notes.about: The false prophets say “Peace” when there is no peace, like men whitewashing a flimsy wall. God says rain, hail and wind will bring the wall down. Then the question “Where is the whitewash with which you covered it?” will become a common taunt, showing up their empty words for all to see.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Where is the whitewash with which you covered it?
figure.means: the false prophets' promises of peace will be shown up as folly when the judgment falls, and men will mock them for it

original.note: In Hebrew the verse is a question that expects a yes: will it not be said to you?

notes.evidence: John Calvin says a common proverb would arise when the wall fell: their folly and vanity would be laid bare, so that the proverb would be current everywhere. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says their vanity and folly would be so plain that it would pass into a proverb, where is the daubing. Both render the words, shall it not be said.
notes.limit: The saying is foretold here, not quoted as already in use.

cites.quote: He confirms the last sentence, namely, that the false prophets would be a laughing-stock to all when their prophecies and divinations came to nothing ... Now the Prophet teaches that a common proverb would arise when the wall fell; for by saying, shall it not be said to them, he signifies that their folly and vanity would be completely exposed, so that this proverb should be everywhere current
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: shall it not be said--Your vanity and folly shall be so manifested that it shall pass into a proverb, "Where is the daubing?"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The useless wood of the vine
notes.about: God asks what vine wood is good for. Nothing can be made of it, not even a peg; it is fuel, and charred it is worth still less. Verse 6 applies it: “so I will give up the people of Jerusalem.” Many read it so: a vine is prized for its fruit, and without fruit His people were worth nothing.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest
figure.means: Jerusalem's people, who had no worth above other nations but what God gave, and having failed to bear fruit were fit only for judgment

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke calls it a parable to humble the Jews' pride: they had nothing but what they received. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): like vine wood, Israel has no superiority and is given to the fire. Matthew Henry calls it a similitude applied to Jerusalem, now unprofitable; Joseph Benson, a parable showing the nation not worth saving; F. Gardiner (Ellicott), a simile showing Israel worthless.
notes.limit: Some read the burned ends and charred middle as judgments Israel had already suffered; the note keeps to the main likeness.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such

notes.short: Two eagles and a vine: a riddle God then explains
notes.about: God has Ezekiel pose a riddle: an eagle takes the top of a cedar; a low vine turns to a second eagle and will wither. figure.name: Riddle
figure.words: A great eagle with great wings and long pinions
figure.means: the king of Babylon, who came to Jerusalem and carried off its king, as verse 12 explains; the second eagle is Egypt’s king

original.note: In Hebrew the verb and the noun share one root: chud chidah, to riddle a riddle.

notes.short: God plants a tender sprig from the cedar
notes.about: After the eagles, God carries the same picture into a promise. He will take a tender sprig from the top of the cedar and plant it on the mountain heights of Israel, where it becomes a majestic cedar that birds of every kind shelter under. The sprig is read as the Messiah from David's royal line.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: I will pluck a tender sprig from its topmost shoots
figure.means: the Messiah, from David's royal house, whom God Himself raises up from a lowly start to a great and lasting kingdom

Matthew Henry: the tree metaphor is carried into the promise, met in part in Zerubbabel, fully in the Messiah. Adam Clarke: a metaphor of the Messiah's kingdom.

notes.short: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes”: a proverb
notes.about: The people quoted a proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge.” By it they claimed to suffer for their fathers’ sins, not their own. The LORD swears they will quote it no more: “The soul who sins is the one who will die.”

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge
figure.means: the fathers sinned and the children bear the punishment, as the people said to put the blame for their judgment on others

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) explains it: the sour grapes are the fathers’ sins, the teeth set on edge the children’s suffering, an error condemned in Jeremiah 31:29-30 too. Henry calls it an evil proverb in common use; F. Gardiner (Ellicott) and G. Currey (Barnes’ Notes), a common saying that put the blame on others. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) and Clarke call it a proverb.
notes.limit: The same proverb is quoted in Jeremiah 31:29. Some writers also call it a parable.

notes.short: A lioness and her cubs: Judah’s kings led captive
notes.about: Ezekiel’s lament tells of a lioness who rears her cubs among lions. One grows into a young lion that devours men; he is trapped and led with hooks to Egypt. A second is caged and brought to the king of Babylon. Many read the lioness as the nation, grown fierce, and her young lions as its kings.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: What was your mother? A lioness among the lions!
figure.means: the nation the kings came from, grown fierce like the nations around; her cubs are its kings, carried off to Egypt and to Babylon

notes.evidence: Clarke calls the chapter two parables: the lioness is Jerusalem, the young lions Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim. Calvin says the prophet uses a likeness drawn from lions, the lioness being the nation. Henry: Judah is compared to a lioness, its kings to her whelps, the first Jehoahaz. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): the mother is the nation, the lion’s ferocity the likeness; the kings, Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin.
notes.limit: Writers differ on details: some take the lioness as Jerusalem, others as the whole nation, and the second young lion as Jehoiakim or as Jehoiachin. All take the first as Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt.

notes.about: The lament’s second picture: the mother is a fruitful vine by the water, with strong branches fit for a ruler’s scepter. figure.words: Your mother was like a vine in your vineyard
figure.means: the nation, once flourishing, whose strong branches are its rulers; uprooted and planted in the wilderness, it is the people carried into exile

figure.words: I am about to ignite in you a fire
figure.means: the judgment the LORD will bring on Judah, the forest being its people and the green and dry trees the righteous and the wicked

notes.short: Samaria and Jerusalem as two unfaithful sisters
notes.about: Ezekiel tells of two sisters who play the harlot from their youth in Egypt, then with Assyria and Babylon, and are punished by their own lovers. God names them: Oholah is Samaria and Oholibah is Jerusalem. The story pictures the two kingdoms turning from God to idols and to foreign powers.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: there were two women, daughters of the same mother
figure.means: Samaria and Jerusalem, the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah; their harlotry is their idolatry and their trust in heathen powers

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the sisters Samaria and Jerusalem are set out in the form of an allegory. notes.short: God's own parable: Jerusalem as a pot on the fire
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to speak a parable: a pot set on the fire, filled with the best pieces of meat and boiled. From verse 6 God explains it: the pot is the city of bloodshed, Jerusalem, put under siege that very day. The meat in it stands for the city's people.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Put the pot on the fire
figure.means: Jerusalem under siege, with its people shut inside like meat in a boiling pot

original.note: In Hebrew the word for parable is mashal, which can also mean a proverb.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verses are called a proverb or parable, the pot with its meat representing Jerusalem and its people, the fire, war. G. notes.limit: Writers also give meanings to the choice pieces and the bones. The note keeps to the main likeness.

notes.short: Ezekiel's wife dies, and he is told not to mourn
notes.about: God takes Ezekiel's wife and forbids him to mourn her. When the people ask what this means, he tells them God will desecrate His sanctuary, the desire of their eyes, and they too will not mourn but waste away in their sins. So Ezekiel will be a sign for them, as the passage itself says.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: you must not mourn or weep or let your tears flow
figure.means: the fall of Jerusalem and the loss of the temple, dearest of all to the people, a grief too deep for the usual mourning

Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a sign in his person of their fate.

notes.short: Tyre pictured as a splendid ship that is wrecked
notes.about: The lament pictures Tyre, the city at the gateway to the sea, as a splendid ship: planks from Senir, a mast of Lebanon cedar, a sail of Egyptian linen, rowers from Sidon and Arvad. Then the east wind shatters it in the heart of the sea, and the sailors on shore mourn its fall.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: They took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you
figure.means: Tyre itself, built up in splendor from the best of many lands; the ship's wreck in the east wind is the city's fall

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke says the prophet paints the city's glory under the allegory of a beautiful ship. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): Tyre is depicted allegorically as a ship, its ruin as a shipwreck by the east wind. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a ship well built and manned, at last wrecked. F. Gardiner (Ellicott's Commentary): a prolonged figure of a ship that is wrecked and sinks.
notes.limit: From verse 9 or 10 to verse 25 the ship gives way to plain words on Tyre's soldiers and trade; the picture returns with the wreck in verse 26.

notes.short: Pharaoh as a Nile monster hauled out on hooks
notes.about: God speaks to Pharaoh as a great monster lying among the Nile's streams, boasting that the river is his. God will put hooks in its jaws, haul it out with the fish clinging to its scales, and leave it in the desert as food for beasts and birds. Many read the fish as his people.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: O great monster who lies among his rivers
figure.means: Pharaoh, proud and secure as lord of Egypt, as the crocodile lies in the Nile as though lord of the river; God will haul him out with hooks

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the crocodile, Egypt's symbol, is here given to Pharaoh, who thought himself lord of Egypt as it seems lord of the Nile; the fish are Egypt's people. F. Gardiner (Ellicott's Commentary): the crocodile stands for Egypt's royal power and the fish its people. Joseph Benson: God carries the metaphor on in the hooks; the fish are his own people pressing him.
notes.limit: The writers call it a figure or a metaphor carried through these verses rather than naming it an allegory. They differ on whether the clinging fish show the people sharing his ruin or turning against him.

The fishes which hang upon the scales of the monster, and are drawn along with it out of the Nile, are the inhabitants of Egypt

notes.short: Assyria the great cedar, held up to Pharaoh
notes.about: Asked who can compare with Pharaoh's greatness, God points to Assyria pictured as a towering cedar, watered by the deep and envied by the trees of Eden, then cut down for its pride. The closing words turn the picture on Egypt: “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude.”

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon
figure.means: Assyria in its greatness, cut down by God for its pride; its fall is set before Pharaoh as a picture of his own

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke: Pharaoh is shown the fall of Nineveh's king under the image of a felled cedar, a picture of his own fate. C. F. notes.short: A watchman's duty pictures Ezekiel's own
notes.about: God gives Ezekiel a case from daily life. A land sets a watchman, and he sees the sword coming. If he blows the horn and a man ignores it, that man's blood is on his own head; if he keeps silent, God holds the watchman to account. In verse 7 God applies it: Ezekiel is Israel's watchman.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: Suppose I bring the sword against a land
figure.means: Ezekiel, whom God set as Israel's watchman: if he warns of judgment, the hearers answer for themselves; if he keeps silent, God holds him to account

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): verses 2 to 6 bring in Ezekiel's duty by an example from life: as a land's watchman must warn of the enemy, so must Ezekiel. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): the earthly watchman's duties come first, then their application to the spiritual one. Joseph Benson: the case illustrates the prophet's duty. Matthew Henry: the office is laid down, then applied to him.
notes.limit: The passage does not call itself a parable; the writers call it an example from life or an illustration. Ezekiel 3:16-21 gives the same charge without the story.

figure.words: Woe to the shepherds of Israel
figure.means: the shepherds are Israel's rulers, who served themselves; the flock is God's people, scattered into exile for want of true care

notes.short: Two sticks joined in one hand: one nation again
notes.about: God tells Ezekiel to write Judah's name on one stick and Joseph's, for the northern tribes, on another, and to join them into one stick in his hand. When the people ask what it means, he is to tell them that God will make the two kingdoms one nation in their land, under one king, His servant David.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: join them together into one stick
figure.means: Israel and Judah, split into two kingdoms, made one nation again in their own land under one king, as verses 19 to 22 explain
